teaser: The world's most famous night scene takes place in broad daylight.

lesson.text: Two things everyone knows about this painting are wrong. It does not happen at night, and nobody in it is on watch. The nickname appeared about a century and a half after Rembrandt painted it, when layers of old varnish had turned the whole surface the color of strong tea.

What Rembrandt delivered in 1642 was a group portrait of an Amsterdam militia, a company of well-off citizens who trained with weapons to defend their city. Their captain, Frans Banninck Cocq, is the man in black. He is giving the order to march. It is daytime.
The darkness here is a painter's choice, not the hour. Rembrandt sends a beam of sun into deep shade so that he can decide exactly what you see first.

Militia portraits were a Dutch specialty, and usually a dull one. Everybody paid a share, so everybody expected to be seen: neat rows of faces, like a class photo. Rembrandt took the same commission and painted the minute before the parade, when no one is yet in place.
The company's weapon was the musket, an early long gun that took many steps to fire. Rembrandt hides a small lesson in how to use one, spread over three men, reading from left to right.

lesson.title: One gun, three steps
lesson.text: Follow the musket across the canvas.

spots.title: Loading
spots.text: The man dressed entirely in red tips powder into the barrel of his musket. He looks down, absorbed in the job.

spots.title: Firing
spots.text: Half hidden behind the captain, a small figure with oak leaves on his helmet lets off a shot in the middle of the crowd. You only see the helmet and the gun.

spots.title: Cleaning
spots.text: Just behind the lieutenant, an older man in a helmet bends over his gun and blows the leftover powder out of its pan.

lesson.text: Those three poses come straight from the drill books of the time. In a manual they are stiff diagrams. Here they become noise: a shot goes off, a drum rolls on the right, pikes clatter overhead. No earlier group portrait had tried to be loud.

The company paid Rembrandt 1,600 guilders, several years of wages for a skilled worker. Each man chipped in about 100, a bit more or less depending on how well he would be shown. Some of them ended up as half a face behind an elbow.

The two leaders got their money's worth. The captain's left hand seems to poke out of the picture toward you. That trick is called foreshortening: drawing something shorter than it is so that it appears to come forward. Beside him walks his lieutenant, dressed in pale yellow.
The captain's outstretched hand casts a shadow. Where does it fall?

spots.title: On the yellow coat
spots.text: The dark shape of fingers lies across the lieutenant's embroidered coat, just below his sash. The shadow ties the two officers together.

lesson.text: That one shadow tells you where the sun is: high on the left, in front of the men. It also shows Rembrandt's favorite tool, chiaroscuro, an Italian word for strong contrast between light and dark. Black suit against yellow suit, lit face against a wall of shade.

At 3.63 by 4.37 meters (about 12 by 14 feet), the canvas is bigger than most living room walls, and the figures in front are life-size. To keep such a mass of people from turning into a traffic jam, Rembrandt organizes it with a few long poles.
Flag, lance and weapons work like arrows.

lines.label: The flag
lines.text: On the left, the flag bearer lifts the company's banner. Its pole leans outward and up, opening the group toward the top corner.

lines.label: The lance
lines.text: On the right, a long lance tilts the other way. Together the two poles spread like an opening fan, with the officers at its hinge.

lines.label: The lieutenant's weapon
lines.text: The lieutenant's short ceremonial spear points down and forward, out of the picture. It aims at the spot where you are standing.

lines.label: The step
lines.text: From the captain's open hand down to his leading foot: the whole company is about to walk forward, off the canvas and into the room.

lesson.text: A fan opening, a step forward. This sense of a scene caught mid-movement, spilling toward the viewer, is what historians call Baroque, the theatrical style of the 1600s. In the militia's hall, the painting hung beside six calmer group portraits by other artists. It must have looked like a door thrown open.

In 1715 the painting moved to Amsterdam's Town Hall, where it did not fit the wall. So it was cut down on all four sides. The left edge lost the most, and two militiamen went with it. We know them only from a small copy made before the trim.

Not everyone here is a paying member. Rembrandt added extras to fill out the crowd: children, a drummer hired for the day, and the strangest figure of all, a girl in a gold dress who glows as if she carried her own lamp.

lesson.title: The extras
lesson.text: Four details that no militiaman paid for.

spots.title: The golden girl
spots.text: She has a child's body and an oddly grown-up face. She is no portrait of a real person: she works as a living emblem of the company, a kind of mascot.

spots.title: The chicken
spots.text: A dead white bird hangs from her belt, claws up. A claw was the symbol of this company, known as the Kloveniers, so she wears their badge.

spots.title: The shield
spots.text: Barely visible on the dark arch, an oval shield lists the names of 18 men who paid. It was added some years later, probably at their request.

spots.title: The dog
spots.text: A thinly painted dog crouches and barks at the drummer. You can see the floor through its body: Rembrandt sketched it with a few light strokes.

lesson.text: Eighteen names on the shield, thirty-four figures on the canvas. The gap is Rembrandt's own cast: sixteen people nobody ordered. He treated a business portrait the way a director treats a stage, and that freedom is what later painters admired most.

A stubborn legend says the militiamen hated the result and that it ruined him. Nothing in the records supports this. The captain even had copies made for himself. Rembrandt's hard years had other causes: his wife Saskia died in 1642, and his spending led to bankruptcy in 1656.
During the Second World War the canvas was taken off its frame, rolled around a cylinder and moved from one hiding place to another. It spent the last years of the war in caves near Maastricht.

It has also been attacked with a knife in 1975 and sprayed with acid in 1990, and repaired both times. Since 2019 the Rijksmuseum has been studying and restoring it inside a glass room, in full view of visitors. In 2021, a computer trained on Rembrandt's style even printed the strips cut off in 1715.

So keep the nickname, everyone does. But the next time you see it, picture the varnish gone and the shutters open: a company of Amsterdam shopkeepers and merchants, stepping out of the shade into the afternoon sun.

quiz.question: Why is the painting called The Night Watch?
options: Darkened varnish made a daytime scene look like night
The militia only patrolled after dark
quiz.explanation: The nickname appeared long after 1642, once old varnish had darkened the surface.

quiz.question: Where does the shadow of the captain's hand fall?
quiz.explanation: The shadow of his fingers lies across the lieutenant's coat, showing the sun is high on the left.

quiz.question: What hangs from the golden girl's belt?
quiz.explanation: The bird's claws refer to the claw emblem of the company, the Kloveniers.

quiz.question: What happened to the painting in 1715?
options: It was slashed with a knife
It was cut down on all sides to fit a wall
quiz.explanation: It was trimmed for the Town Hall, losing two figures on the left.

quiz.question: What does “chiaroscuro” mean?
options: Strong contrast between light and dark
Drawing an object shorter so it comes forward
A portrait of a whole group
quiz.explanation: Chiaroscuro is the Italian word for strong contrast of light and dark.

quiz.question: How many names are listed on the shield?
quiz.explanation: Eighteen men paid; the other figures are extras Rembrandt added.

facts.text: Every figure in The Night Watch is a militiaman who paid for his portrait.
facts.explanation: Only 18 names are on the shield; Rembrandt added many extras, including the girl and the drummer.

facts.text: Three men in the painting show three steps of handling a musket.
facts.explanation: One loads, one fires and one blows the pan clean, as in the drill books of the time.

facts.text: Records show that the militia rejected the painting and that it ruined Rembrandt.
facts.explanation: That is a legend: nothing in the records supports it, and the captain had copies made.
